doctrines/baptism/question: Who should be baptised, how, in whose name — and what does baptism actually do?
doctrines/baptism/summary: Christians agree that Christ commanded baptism, but divide over infants or believers only, immersion or pouring, sacramental regeneration or symbolic testimony, the baptismal formula, and whether baptism in the Holy Spirit is a second experience after conversion.
doctrines/baptism/longText:
Baptism is the one rite that almost every Christian body shares, and most churches recognise each other’s baptisms in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The earliest evidence — the Didache, Justin Martyr, Tertullian, Hippolytus’ Apostolic Tradition and the third-century baptistery at Dura-Europos — shows a rite of catechesis, renunciation, immersion (or, where needed, pouring) in the triune name, anointing and first communion, understood as new birth, illumination and the forgiveness of sins.

Infant baptism appears by about 200: Tertullian counsels delay, Origen calls it apostolic, and Cyprian’s council (c.253) refuses to make infants wait. Augustine’s use of infant baptism against Pelagius tied it to original sin, and by the early Middle Ages infant baptism was universal in East and West. The East kept triple immersion with chrismation and infant communion; the West gradually adopted pouring and sprinkling and separated confirmation.

The Reformation reopened everything. Luther kept infant baptism as God’s regenerating Word in water; Zwingli, Bullinger and Calvin reinterpreted it as the sign and seal of the covenant of grace, parallel to circumcision. The Swiss Brethren drew the opposite conclusion: on 21 January 1525 in Zurich they baptised believers, and the Anabaptist movement — defined at Schleitheim (1527) and later by Menno Simons — was savagely persecuted by Catholics and Protestants alike. English Separatists in Amsterdam (Smyth, 1609) founded the Baptist tradition, which later insisted on immersion. Quakers abandoned outward baptism altogether.

In 19th-century America the Stone-Campbell movement taught immersion "for the remission of sins"; the Holiness movement spoke of a "baptism of the Holy Ghost" after conversion, which Pentecostals (Topeka 1901, Azusa Street 1906) linked with speaking in tongues; and the 1913-16 "New Issue" produced Oneness Pentecostals who baptise "in Jesus’ name" and reject the Trinity. In the 20th century scholars such as James Dunn argued that Spirit-baptism belongs to conversion itself, and the WCC’s Baptism, Eucharist and Ministry (1982) charted a remarkable ecumenical convergence while leaving the infant/believer divide unresolved.
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/0/label: What is baptism, who should receive it, how, and what does it do?
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/0/text: All major Christian traditions baptise in water (Quakers and the Salvation Army are notable exceptions), and most recognise one another’s Trinitarian baptisms. They disagree on the subjects (infants or believers), the mode (immersion, pouring, sprinkling), the effect (regeneration, sign and seal, or public testimony), the formula, and how "baptism in the Holy Spirit" relates to water baptism.
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/1/text: "Baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost"; "He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved." The Trinitarian formula and the faith-baptism sequence.
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/2/label: Acts 2:38-41; 22:16 — for the remission of sins
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/2/text: "Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost … For the promise is unto you, and to your children." Key for regeneration, Restorationist, Oneness and paedobaptist arguments alike.
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/3/text: Lydia "and her household", the jailer "and all his"; children of a believer are "holy". Paedobaptists read households as including infants; credobaptists note no infant is mentioned.
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/4/text: "Buried with him by baptism into death"; "circumcised with the circumcision made without hands … buried with him in baptism." The basis for immersion symbolism and for the covenant-circumcision analogy.
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/5/label: John 3:5; Titus 3:5; 1 Peter 3:21 — water, Spirit and new birth
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/5/text: "Born of water and of the Spirit"; "the washing of regeneration"; "baptism doth also now save us … the answer of a good conscience toward God." Central to baptismal regeneration and to its critics.
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/6/text: Samaritans baptised but receiving the Spirit later; Cornelius receiving the Spirit before water; "by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body". The texts of the subsequence debate.
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/7/label: Didache: living water, or pour thrice
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/7/text: The early church manual directs baptism "into the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, in living water", permitting other water and, if necessary, pouring water three times on the head; baptiser and candidate fast beforehand.
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/8/text: Believers who have been taught, pray and fast are "regenerated" in water in the triune name.
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/9/label: Tertullian: little fishes — and delay for children
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/9/text: The first treatise on baptism defends its necessity but counsels delay for little children and the unmarried — the first evidence that infants were being baptised.
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/10/label: Origen and Cyprian: infant baptism as apostolic tradition
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/10/text: Origen calls infant baptism a tradition from the apostles; Cyprian’s African council (c.253) rules that newborns need not wait until the eighth day.
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/11/label: Cyril of Jerusalem: your grave and your mother
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/11/text: Easter mystagogy describes renunciation, triple immersion and anointing: the font as tomb and womb.
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/12/label: Creed of Constantinople (381): "one baptism for the remission of sins"
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/12/text: The Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed confesses one, unrepeatable baptism; the Donatist and rebaptism controversies settle that Trinitarian baptism by heretics or schismatics is not repeated.
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/13/text: Infants are baptised for the remission of (original) sin and regenerated; East and West baptise infants, the East with chrismation and communion.
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/14/text: God gives new birth and forgiveness through the water joined to the Word: Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and (for believers) Restorationist teaching.
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/15/text: The East keeps triple immersion; the medieval West moves toward affusion (pouring) and aspersion (sprinkling); Baptists later insist on immersion as of the essence.
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/16/text: Zwingli and Bullinger argue that, as Israel’s infants received circumcision, the children of believers receive baptism as the sign of the one covenant of grace (Col 2:11-12; Acts 2:39).
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/17/text: Hubmaier and the Swiss Brethren reply that Christ commanded teaching, faith, then baptism; no infant baptism appears in the New Testament; and baptism is the pledge of a good conscience (1 Pet 3:21).
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/18/label: First adult baptisms in Zurich (21 January 1525)
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/18/text: After the Zurich council orders infants baptised, Conrad Grebel baptises George Blaurock in Felix Manz’s house; the Anabaptist movement begins.
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/19/text: Baptism is the sign and seal of the covenant of grace given to believers and their children; its efficacy is tied to God’s promise and the Spirit’s timing.
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/20/text: Baptism upon confession, as entry into a disciplined, separated community.
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/21/text: Swiss Brethren agree seven articles, beginning with believers’ baptism.
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/22/text: Felix Manz is drowned in the Limmat (5 January 1527), Michael Sattler burned (May 1527); Catholic and Protestant authorities execute thousands under imperial law (Speyer, 1529); the Münster debacle (1534-35) hardens hostility.
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/23/label: Trent, Session VII (1547): canons on baptism
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/23/text: Trent anathematises denial of infant baptism, rebaptism of those baptised as infants, and the view that baptism is not necessary for salvation.
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/24/text: John Smyth (1609) and Thomas Helwys (1612) found Baptist churches; Particular Baptists adopt immersion (c.1641).
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/25/text: Believers’ baptism spreads with Baptist missions (William Carey, 1792) and later with Pentecostal and many evangelical and independent churches worldwide.
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/26/text: Friends hold that the one baptism is the inward baptism of the Spirit and practise no outward rite (Barclay, Apology, 1676).
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/27/label: Stone-Campbell: immersion for the remission of sins
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/27/text: Believers are immersed "for the remission of sins"; baptism is the point of pardon.
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/28/label: Spirit baptism as a subsequent experience
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/28/text: Holiness and Pentecostal teaching: after conversion, believers should seek baptism in the Spirit for power, evidenced (for classical Pentecostals) by tongues.
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/29/text: From the 1913 Arroyo Seco camp meeting, some Pentecostals re-baptise "in the name of Jesus" and adopt a non-Trinitarian Oneness doctrine of God.
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/30/text: The AoG adopts a Trinitarian Statement of Fundamental Truths; about a quarter of its ministers leave to form Oneness bodies (later the United Pentecostal Church, 1945).
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/31/text: Reformed, Baptist and many evangelical scholars hold that every believer is baptised in the Spirit at conversion; subsequent experiences are fillings.
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/32/text: The WCC Faith and Order text records convergence: baptism as participation in Christ’s death and resurrection, unrepeatable, with infant and believers’ baptism both seen as legitimate expressions within a lifelong process; calls for mutual recognition. Many churches now issue mutual recognition agreements (e.g. Germany, Magdeburg 2007).
doctrines/baptism/flow/nodes/33/text: Most of the world’s Christians (Catholic, Orthodox, Oriental, Lutheran, Anglican, Reformed, Methodist) baptise infants; Baptists, Pentecostals, most independent and Global South evangelical churches baptise believers, usually by immersion; Pentecostal-charismatic Spirit-baptism experience is shared by hundreds of millions; Oneness Pentecostals (outside Nicene orthodoxy) baptise in Jesus’ name.
doctrines/holy-spirit/name: The Holy Spirit and the Gifts
doctrines/holy-spirit/question: Does the Holy Spirit still give miraculous gifts, and how do believers receive the Spirit?
doctrines/holy-spirit/summary: All Christians confess the Holy Spirit as "Lord and Giver of Life". They differ sharply over whether prophecy, tongues and healing continue, whether Spirit-baptism is a second experience evidenced by tongues, and who may speak with prophetic or apostolic authority, from the Montanist crisis to Pentecostalism, the charismatic renewal and today’s prosperity and apostolic movements.
doctrines/holy-spirit/longText:
The New Testament presents the Spirit as the gift of the last days: poured out at Pentecost with tongues and prophecy, distributing gifts "to every man severally as he will" (1 Cor 12:11), and producing love, joy and peace. Second-century writers such as Justin and Irenaeus describe prophecy and healing in their churches as a matter of course. But the New Prophecy of Montanus, Priscilla and Maximilla in Phrygia (from c.156), with its ecstatic first-person oracles and claim to the Paraclete’s final discipline, forced the Church to decide how prophecy relates to apostolic tradition. The first recorded synods rejected it, and suspicion of ecstatic prophecy deepened.

In the 4th century the focus shifted to the Spirit’s divinity, confessed at Constantinople (381) as "the Lord and Giver of Life ... who spake by the prophets". Chrysostom and the young Augustine observed that the Corinthian gifts no longer occurred, though Augustine later recorded many healings. Eastern Christianity never developed a doctrine of cessation: holy elders, wonder-working saints and mystics such as Symeon the New Theologian kept alive an expectation of conscious experience of the Spirit. In the West, miracles were associated with saints and relics, and the Reformers, confronting both Catholic miracle claims and radical "enthusiasts", argued that the gospel needed no new miracles: the seed of Protestant cessationism, systematised by B. B. Warfield in 1918.

Wesleyan teaching on a second work of grace and the 19th-century Holiness movement prepared the ground for Pentecostalism. In 1901 Charles Parham taught that tongues were the evidence of Spirit-baptism; from 1906 the Azusa Street revival led by William J. Seymour sent missionaries worldwide, alongside parallel revivals in Wales, India, Korea and Chile. From 1960 the charismatic renewal brought Pentecostal experience into Anglican, Lutheran and Catholic churches; the 1980s "Third Wave" brought it to evangelicals; and since the 1970s the Word of Faith and prosperity teachings and the New Apostolic Reformation have generated intense controversy.

Today Pentecostal and charismatic Christians number perhaps 600–650 million, concentrated in Africa, Latin America and Asia. The debates (cessationism versus continuationism, initial evidence, the testing of prophecy, prosperity and apostolic authority) are among the most practically consequential in world Christianity, shaping worship, healing ministry, mission and even politics. This section sets out each view in the words its adherents would recognise before giving its critics’ objections.
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/0/label: Does the Holy Spirit still give miraculous gifts, and how do believers receive the Spirit?
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/0/text: Pentecost poured out the Spirit with tongues, prophecy and healings. Did these gifts cease with the apostles, or continue? Is there a distinct "baptism in the Spirit" after conversion, and is it evidenced by tongues? Who may speak in the Spirit’s name today, and how is prophecy tested?
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/1/label: Joel 2:28–32 and Acts 2: "I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh"
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/1/text: Peter interprets Pentecost’s tongues as Joel’s promise for "the last days" and "to all that are afar off" (Acts 2:39). Pentecostals read Acts 2, 8, 10 and 19 as a pattern; others as unrepeatable salvation-historical firsts.
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/2/label: John 14–16: the Paraclete who will guide into all truth
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/2/text: Jesus promises "another Comforter" who will teach and "guide you into all truth" (John 16:13). Montanists and Joachites claimed new Paraclete revelation; the wider Church insisted the Spirit witnesses to Christ and does not add to the apostolic faith.
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/3/label: 1 Corinthians 12–14: varieties of gifts, one Spirit
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/3/text: Paul lists wisdom, knowledge, faith, healings, miracles, prophecy, discernment, tongues and interpretation (12:8–10), asks "do all speak with tongues?" (12:30), and says prophecies and tongues will cease "when that which is perfect is come" (13:8–10), which cessationists have read as the completed canon or apostolic era, and continuationists as Christ’s return.
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/4/label: Irenaeus: brethren in the Church prophesy and speak in tongues
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/4/text: Irenaeus treats prophecy, tongues and even raising the dead as continuing in the catholic Church of his day, against Gnostic claims to secret gifts.
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/5/text: In Phrygia, Montanus and the prophetesses Priscilla and Maximilla speak ecstatically in the first person as the Paraclete, call for stricter fasting and readiness for martyrdom, and point to Pepuza as the New Jerusalem.
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/6/label: Objection: ecstatic, first-person prophecy breaks with tradition
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/6/text: Anonymous and Apollonius (in Eusebius) and Miltiades argue that true prophets do not speak in ecstasy or frenzy, that the prophetesses left their husbands and took gifts, and that their predictions failed.
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/7/label: Asian synods excommunicate the New Prophecy (c.177)
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/7/text: The first recorded church synods in Asia Minor examine and reject the New Prophecy; Rome, after hesitation, follows (c.200). Montanist communities survive in Phrygia until Justinian’s persecution in the 6th century.
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/8/text: The Carthaginian theologian embraces the Paraclete’s new discipline (no remarriage, stricter fasting, no flight in persecution), while remaining orthodox on the Trinity.
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/9/label: Basil and Constantinople 381: the Spirit is "Lord and Giver of Life"
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/9/text: The debate shifts from gifts to the Spirit’s person: Basil defends worship of the Spirit "with" the Father and Son; the Creed of 381 confesses the Spirit "who spake by the prophets".
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/10/labe: Chrysostom and Augustine: the signs "were adapted to the time"
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/10/text: Late-4th-century fathers observe that the Corinthian gifts no longer occur in their churches and treat tongues as a sign for the Church’s founding era.
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/11/labe: Augustine revises: "even now miracles are wrought"
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/11/text: In City of God 22.8 Augustine catalogues healings in Hippo and corrects his earlier view, a passage both sides cite.
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/12/labe: Symeon the New Theologian: conscious experience of the Spirit
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/12/text: The Byzantine mystic insists that baptism in the Spirit must be consciously experienced, often with tears and vision of divine light, an Eastern current later valued by charismatics. Eastern Orthodoxy never formally adopted cessationism; miracles of saints and holy elders remain expected.
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/13/text: Confronted by the Zwickau prophets and Karlstadt, Luther insists the Spirit comes through the external Word and sacraments, not apart from them. Reformers counter Catholic appeals to miracles by arguing that new miracles are unnecessary to confirm an old gospel.
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/14/text: B. B. Warfield’s Counterfeit Miracles (1918) systematises Reformation instincts: sign-gifts authenticated the apostles and ceased with them and the closed canon.
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/15/labe: Wesley: the gifts waned because love grew cold
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/15/text: Wesley’s theology of a second work of grace (entire sanctification) became, through the Holiness movement, the template for a post-conversion "baptism in the Spirit".
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/16/text: At Bethel Bible School, Topeka, Agnes Ozman speaks in tongues on 1 January 1901; Charles Parham teaches tongues as the "Bible evidence" of Spirit baptism.
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/17/text: Under the African American preacher William J. Seymour, a multiracial revival in Los Angeles sends missionaries worldwide; parallel outpourings occur in Wales (1904), India (Mukti, 1905), Korea (Pyongyang, 1907) and Chile (Valparaíso, 1909).
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/18/labe: Assemblies of God fixes "initial physical evidence" (1916)
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/18/text: The AG Statement of Fundamental Truths (1916) makes tongues the initial physical sign of Spirit baptism, a doctrinal boundary for classical Pentecostalism; some Pentecostals (e.g. the Chilean Methodist Pentecostal Church) never adopted it.
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/19/text: All the gifts of 1 Corinthians 12 remain available until Christ returns, though not tied to a second experience or to tongues as evidence; represented in Grudem’s Four Views (1996).
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/20/labe: Charismatic renewal in the historic churches
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/20/text: Dennis Bennett, an Episcopal rector in Van Nuys, announces he has spoken in tongues (1960); renewal spreads to Lutherans, Anglicans and, from the Duquesne weekend (1967), Catholics.
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/21/labe: Rome welcomes the Catholic Charismatic Renewal (1975)
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/21/text: Paul VI addresses 10,000 charismatics in St Peter’s at Pentecost 1975, calling the renewal a "chance for the Church"; Cardinal Suenens’ Malines Documents (1974) interpret "baptism in the Spirit" as a release of sacramental grace. Later popes, including Francis (CHARIS, 2019), affirm it.
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/22/text: John Wimber and C. Peter Wagner’s Fuller course MC510 (1982) and the Vineyard: signs and wonders for ordinary evangelicals, without a second-blessing theology.
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/23/text: Holy laughter and other manifestations at the Toronto Airport Vineyard draw hundreds of thousands; in December 1995 the Association of Vineyard Churches withdraws its endorsement over concerns about the focus on manifestations.
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/24/labe: Word of Faith and the prosperity gospel
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/24/text: Kenneth Hagin’s Rhema Bible Training Center (1974), Kenneth Copeland and Oral Roberts’ "seed faith" teach that faith-filled confession secures health and wealth; exported to Africa, Latin America and Asia.
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/25/text: Wagner’s networks of contemporary apostles and prophets, the "Seven Mountains" mandate, strategic-level spiritual warfare.
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/26/labe: Objections: Lausanne, Pentecostal scholars and NAR critics
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/26/text: The Lausanne Cape Town Commitment (2010) rejects the excesses of the prosperity gospel as contrary to biblical teaching on suffering, generosity and the poor; Pentecostal scholars such as Gordon Fee had already called health-and-wealth teaching a "disease" (1985); critics of the NAR (Geivett and Pivec, 2014) challenge governing apostles and failed prophecies, e.g. about the 2020 US election.
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/27/text: Pentecostal, charismatic and independent Spirit-movements grow from a few million in 1910 to hundreds of millions, above all in Africa, Latin America and Asia (Yoido Full Gospel Church, Seoul; Redeemed Christian Church of God, Nigeria; Brazilian Assemblies of God), reshaping worship, healing ministry and social mobility.
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/28/text: The World Christian Database counts roughly 600–650 million Pentecostals and charismatics (c.2020), about a quarter of all Christians. Cessationism remains strong in confessional Reformed and some Baptist circles (e.g. Strange Fire conference, 2013); most evangelical scholars are "open but cautious" continuationists; Catholic and Orthodox churches acknowledge charisms within sacramental order. Fresh revivals (Asbury, 2023) and debates over prophecy, prosperity and apostolic authority continue.
doctrines/holy-spirit/flow/nodes/29/text: A chapel service at a Wesleyan-Holiness university in Kentucky extends into two weeks of continuous worship, notable for its deliberate lack of celebrity leadership and manifestations, illustrating a quieter, Holiness-style expectation of the Spirit.
